A more consequential opening has emerged in quantum memory. Building on an existing 3D passive-memory proposal, we have a candidate construction that replaces its higher-body interactions with local three-body qubit interactions while retaining long-lived thermal storage under a specified noise model. Two internal reviews have checked different parts of the argument and caught corrections that are being incorporated. If the full proof holds, this would make an abstract protected-memory design closer to the kinds of interactions hardware can implement. It is not yet a practical memory: the required temperature and interaction strengths may be extremely demanding, and efficient initialization and robustness to general hardware errors remain open. It has not had external review.
evidence.range_scope: Complete candidate memory/resource update,approximately07:14 observation after07:05marker;partial reviews/corrections and loading obstruction retain source scope.

evidence.quote: I’ve put the quantum-memory construction through a stricter resource check. The proof’s current sufficient temperature scale is extraordinarily small, and I cannot yet show how to load a qubit into the required thermal state efficiently. The very small bound is a conservative proof guarantee, not a demonstrated physical lower limit. So my assessment is: potentially meaningful mathematics about which interactions can retain a thermal memory, but not yet a credible practical memory breakthrough. The next attack is the actual write/loading operation and whether the resource bounds can be improved.
evidence.range_scope: Complete candidate memory/resource update,approximately07:14 observation after07:05marker;partial reviews/corrections and loading obstruction retain source scope.

evidence.quote: There’s a useful improvement to the quantum-memory route: a different three-body qubit construction has an internally checked energy-scale guarantee more than 100 million times larger than the first one. It uses more connections between the auxiliary qubits, so that gain has a hardware cost. The important caveat is that the actual memory temperature requirement is still much colder than that number alone suggests, and we still haven’t established efficient, fault-tolerant writing or robustness to general hardware noise. So I’m not yet calling it a practical memory.
evidence.range_scope: Complete distinct-variant energy-scale comparison,extra auxiliary connections,temperature and fault-tolerant writing/general-noise limits;not a temperature factor.

evidence.quote: The memory work has made progress on the noise question: we now have an internally checked extension for a specified class of microscopic interacting baths, rather than relying only on an idealized noise equation. It still assumes a particular correlated thermal starting state and an ideal write/read interface. That makes the storage argument stronger, but it does not solve the practical task of preparing that state or writing into it reliably. The result is also not a guarantee against arbitrary hardware noise. I’m focusing on those missing operations.
evidence.range_scope: Complete checked microscopic-bath storage extension,particular correlated thermal start and ideal I/O assumptions;not arbitrary hardware-noise/preparation/writing theorem.

evidence.quote: On the memory’s loading problem, we now have an internally checked ideal preparation method for the auxiliary part, including its thermal fluctuations. That removes one of the missing pieces I mentioned earlier. It does not yet prepare the complete memory state: the correct distribution of the memory’s error patterns still has to be generated, and noisy writing remains unresolved. The sufficient operating conditions for this version are also extremely demanding, so there is still no practical device claim.
evidence.range_scope: Complete chronological source-reported internal ideal preparation check;auxiliary step then complete isolated state,not noisy writing or joint bath preparation.

evidence.quote: A meaningful update on the memory: we now have an internally checked ideal preparation procedure for the complete isolated memory state, not just its auxiliaries. It combines a way to sample the required error patterns with the auxiliary preparation, and is designed to preserve a qubit entangled with another system. This closes a mathematical loading step I previously said was missing. It still assumes ideal active controls and extremely demanding fixed operating conditions. Reliable noisy writing, preparation together with the actual bath, and a practical advantage over active error correction remain unproved. The result has not been externally reviewed.
evidence.range_scope: Complete chronological source-reported internal ideal preparation check;auxiliary step then complete isolated state,not noisy writing or joint bath preparation.

evidence.quote: The next memory test exposed why noisy writing is harder than it first appeared: a fault in one auxiliary component can reverse a neighbouring component’s preferred state. That means the equilibrium storage proof cannot simply be extended by treating faulty components as missing checks. This is not a proof that the memory fails. It rules out a shortcut we were testing. The ideal preparation result still stands under its stated assumptions; I’m now working on whether real faults remain sufficiently contained during the full write-and-hold process.
evidence.range_scope: Complete noisy-writing fault update rejects missing-check shortcut only;not memory failure or invalidation of ideal preparation.
